clue.text: Appeared embarrassed

definitions.meaning: turned up or arrived, as a guest does at a party
made someone look foolish by outdoing or exposing them

explanation.definitionFit: To turn up is one sense of the phrasal verb; to humiliate someone by comparison is the other.

clue.text: Sari they stitched together creating frenzied excitement

indicators.note: pieces stitched together are joined into a new shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Two women sew a sari, causing great excitement.
explanation.definitionFit: Hysteria is uncontrollable emotion, wild agitation in a crowd or person.

clue.text: Talk of enjoying a couple of days where there's no stress, in a word

definitions.text: where there's no stress, in a word

indicators.note: talk of says the words are spoken, so their sound gives the answer

parts.note: spending Saturday and Sunday away is weekending

explanation.surface: Chat about a relaxing two days off without pressure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no stress' looks like relaxation; it is the prosody term. In verse, an ending whose last syllable is unstressed is a weak ending.
explanation.definitionFit: In prosody a line or word finishing on an unaccented syllable has this kind of close.

clue.text: At rear of shop, I serve bent goods taken from back of lorry?

definitions.text: goods taken from back of lorry?

indicators.note: at the rear of the shop word means placed after it

parts.note: a deli is a delicatessen, a kind of shop

indicators.note: bent means twisted out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Behind a shop, someone hands over dodgy goods that fell off a lorry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bent' rearranges ISERVE into VERIES. Goods 'from the back of a lorry' sounds stolen in British slang, but here they are simply unloaded.
explanation.definitionFit: Parcels unloaded at a door are what a courier drops off; the question mark admits the slang twist.

clue.text: Has a lot to say about Ireland's principal crop

indicators.note: about means going round, so one word surrounds another

parts.note: to prate is to talk at length foolishly

indicators.note: the principal letter of a word is its first, of Ireland's

explanation.surface: Someone talks at length about potatoes, the staple harvest of Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: PRATIES is an Irish dialect word for potatoes, fitting the surface's Irish setting.
explanation.definitionFit: Potatoes are the harvest meant; this dialect word names them.

clue.text: Small measure taken to rein in a cleric

annotationWithheld.why: Small measure taken to rein in a cleric (4): IMAM reads as IM(A)M, but no reading of 'Small measure taken' gives IMM, and no blog parse was found
annotationWithheld.clue: Small measure taken to rein in a cleric

clue.text: Island hunter's unlikely aim?

parts.note: what a hunter wants is to bag game
an aim of nothing, zero, is no hunter's goal

explanation.surface: A question about what a hunter would hardly set out to do.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as 'to bag nothing': a hunter's aim is to bag something, so bagging O is an unlikely aim.
explanation.definitionFit: Tobago is the Caribbean island paired with Trinidad.

clue.text: Concerned over safe in which there's a firearm

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means placed above, so this piece comes first

parts.note: re means concerning or about

indicators.note: in which there's says one piece is held inside another

parts.note: peter is old criminal slang for a safe

explanation.surface: Worried about a strongbox that contains a gun.
explanation.walkthrough: PETER is old criminal slang for a safe; 'over' works because this is a down clue, so the first piece sits above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A repeater is a gun that fires several shots without reloading.

clue.text: Be easily first to introduce ridiculous speed limit in the capital?

indicators.note: to introduce something in a place is to put it inside, so these letters go within the city

parts.note: Rome is the capital of Italy
a limit of zero miles per hour would be absurd: O (zero) plus MPH

explanation.surface: A complaint about a silly new traffic restriction imposed on a city's streets.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a real traffic rule; a limit of 0 mph is the absurd one meant. The question mark flags that 'the capital' is one example of a capital city.
explanation.definitionFit: Winning a race by a long margin, comfortably ahead of the field, is the idiom's sense.

clue.text: Extremely anxious, put to sea in storm

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its first and last letters, taken from the word anxious

parts.note: to set out on a voyage is to sail

explanation.surface: A nervous sailor sets out despite a gale blowing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'storm' looks like weather to sail into; here it is a verb, to attack a stronghold.
explanation.definitionFit: To storm a castle is to attack it violently, a synonym of the verb.

clue.text: Bully's identity protected by friend

indicators.note: something protected by another is surrounded and shielded by it, so one word sits inside the other

parts.note: an intimate is a close friend
ID is the usual short form of identity, as on an ID card

explanation.surface: A thug's real name is kept secret by an accomplice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bully' looks like a noun, a thug; here it is the verb. The 's after it is a link meaning 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: To bully someone is to frighten them into submission, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Allotment would be slightly too much for this old lady

indicators.text: would be slightly too much for this
indicators.note: the allotment word has one letter more than this one needs, so a letter is dropped from it

parts.note: a grant is a sum allotted to someone

explanation.surface: An elderly woman finds a vegetable plot a little more than she can manage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Allotment' suggests a garden plot, but it means an allowance, GRANT; one letter too many means dropping the final T.
explanation.definitionFit: Gran is an informal name for a grandmother, whom family might jokingly call the old lady.

clue.text: Date for getting rid of inequalities

definitions.meaning: an arranged social engagement, a night out with someone
making things level or fair, smoothing out differences

explanation.definitionFit: A night spent out socially is one sense; levelling differences, as in a phrasal verb, is the other.

clue.text: Vague sort of article

definitions.meaning: in grammar, 'a' and 'an' make up one kind of article, as against 'the'

explanation.definitionFit: Unclear or unsettled is one sense; grammar's term for 'a' or 'an' as against 'the' is the other.

clue.text: We hear dogsbody was willing to supply timber

indicators.note: we hear says the words are judged by their sound

parts.note: a gofer is a dogsbody who runs errands, and would means was willing

explanation.surface: An errand-runner offered to fetch some wood.
explanation.walkthrough: Gopher wood is the timber Noah's ark was built from in Genesis.
explanation.definitionFit: This biblical wood is a kind of timber, the material of the ark.

clue.text: Jewish group keeps Israel's leader unenlightened

parts.note: to keep something is to have it

indicators.note: a word's leader is its first letter, here of Israel's

parts.note: dim means slow-witted or ignorant

explanation.surface: A religious sect is accused of keeping a national leader in the dark.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hasidim are a strictly orthodox Jewish movement founded in eighteenth-century Poland.

clue.text: Printout of work with introductory chapter penned by English author

indicators.note: penned means enclosed, as in a pen, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: Thomas Hardy is the English novelist

indicators.note: introductory puts the chapter letter at the front of the work

parts.note: OP is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: A printed copy of a book whose opening chapter an English novelist wrote.
explanation.walkthrough: HARDY is Thomas Hardy, the novelist of Wessex; 'introductory' puts the chapter letter before the work, and the pair is enclosed.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard copy is the paper version of a document, as opposed to a file on screen.

clue.text: One may take issue with a duke, sozzled toper

indicators.note: a sozzled person is drunk, so these letters stagger into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone argues with an aristocrat and a drunken boozer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sozzled' rearranges TOPER into OPTER. 'take issue' looks like disagreeing, but issue means children: an adopter takes in someone else's offspring.
explanation.definitionFit: Issue is a legal word for offspring, and someone who adopts takes a child into their family.

clue.text: Calm sea late in the day?

parts.note: even means level and unruffled
the tide is the sea's rise and fall

explanation.surface: A quiet sea as evening falls.
explanation.definitionFit: Eventide is a poetic word for evening, the close of the day.

clue.text: Bet inhaling dope is painful

indicators.note: inhaling means taking in, so one word holds another

parts.note: a punt is a bet
dope and gen both mean information

explanation.surface: A gambler smoking drugs is in a bad way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dope' suggests drugs; it means information, GEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Pungent can mean sharp and stinging, causing a pricking sensation.

clue.text: Four thugs thumped female … An example of this?

indicators.note: thumped means beaten up, so the letters are knocked about into a new order

explanation.surface: A gang of four men beat up a woman, an act of violence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'thumped' rearranges FOURTHUGS plus F. The definition points back at the clue: thugs beating someone up is an instance of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Rough stuff means violent behaviour, and the scene painted is a case of it.

clue.text: Analyse new film showing in this country

indicators.note: a film showing in a place is inside it, so these letters go within the other piece

parts.note: for a British newspaper this country is the UK
pic is slang for a film

explanation.surface: Review a fresh movie being screened in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: To unpick an argument is to take it apart and examine it closely.

clue.text: Some people denigrate the prime minister

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A remark that certain people disparage the head of government.
explanation.walkthrough: The prime minister meant is Anthony Eden, British prime minister from 1955 to 1957.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Eden served as British prime minister in the 1950s, so the name stands for that office holder.

clue.text: Frank accompanies old woman in church near northern city

indicators.note: one group of letters is placed in another, held between its letters

parts.note: CE is the abbreviation for the Church of England
frank means open and candid
a hag is an ugly old woman

explanation.surface: Frank escorts an elderly lady inside a church in the north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank' reads as a man's name; it is the adjective, OPEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Copenhagen is the capital city of Denmark.

clue.text: Wig's removed at first to reveal skin

indicators.note: its first letter is taken away from the scolding word

parts.note: to wig is to scold or chide

explanation.surface: A hairpiece taken off shows the scalp beneath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wig' looks like a hairpiece; it is the verb to scold, CHIDE, minus its first letter. The 's is a link meaning 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A hide is an animal's skin, especially a large one.

clue.text: Single party member in charge is much revered

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
a Con is a member of the UK Conservative Party

explanation.surface: One politician who heads the party is worshipped.
explanation.definitionFit: Something iconic is treated as a symbol and held in great esteem.

clue.text: Broken containers, say

indicators.note: say signals that the clue words are spoken and their sound gives the answer

parts.note: a pack and a tin are both containers, giving two words side by side

explanation.surface: Damaged boxes, for instance.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken quickly, PACK TIN runs together and the T sounds like the D of the answer. 'Broken' means stopped working, as a machine has when it gives up.
explanation.definitionFit: A machine that has failed is said, informally, to have given up the ghost in this phrasal sense.

clue.text: Machine parts dealers distributed by the ton

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for ton

indicators.note: letters distributed are spread out and dealt again, so the word dealers is rearranged

explanation.surface: Traders hand out goods in large quantities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'distributed' rearranges DEALERS into READLES; 'by' places T beside it, at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Treadles are foot-operated levers that drive sewing machines and lathes.
